Ray: Good morning, nerds. It's Friday, November twentieth, twenty twenty six, and this is Nerd News Radio. I'm Ray.

Ada: And I'm Ada, here to ask the annoying questions.

Ray: Today's lead: can counting the islands and holes in magnetic domains tell you something new about a phase transition?

Lead story

Ray: Okay, so. The Ising model is the classic toy magnet. Spins on a lattice, each one up or down, and at a certain temperature the whole thing flips from disordered to ordered. Physicists usually track things like magnetization. This paper asks whether the shape of the domains, the patches of up spins and patches of down spins, carries extra information.

Ada: Shape, how?

Ray: Topology. The authors build a cell complex for the up domains and another for the down domains, then take the difference of their Euler characteristics. Roughly, that's a number that tracks how many separate pieces and holes you have. They also derive an expression linking it to ordinary Ising quantities, so they can understand its behavior physically.

Ada: Did they measure it, or just derive it?

Ray: Both. They ran Monte Carlo simulations, which means randomly sampling spin configurations, on square and triangular lattices. They combined that with multihistogram reweighting, a trick for reusing simulation data to estimate results at nearby temperatures. Then finite size scaling, which means watching how a susceptibility peak shifts as the lattice grows.

Ada: And the result?

Ray: The observable behaves like an order parameter near the ferromagnetic transition. Its susceptibility gives pseudocritical temperatures that converge to the known critical temperature on both lattices. And a byproduct: at any finite positive temperature, the expected Euler characteristic exceeds a positive bound that doesn't depend on lattice size. That disproves a previously suggested conjecture.

Ada: Here's my question. Is it better than plain magnetization?

Ray: Not according to the abstract. On the square lattice, the leading estimate of the critical exponent depends more strongly on the fitting range than the magnetization estimate does. The authors say that's consistent with stronger subleading finite size corrections, meaning extra terms that fade as systems get bigger, and fits with an added correction term support that. The triangular lattice result is cut off in my text, so I can't tell you.

Ada: So a different lens, not a sharper one.

Ray: That's interpretation, but I think it's fair. Why it matters: it tests whether the topology of microscopic configurations adds insight beyond standard thermodynamic observables, and it does it in the one model where we already know the answers.

Magnets and materials

Ray: On to magnets. A paper in the Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials derives anisotropy energy functions for all point groups, up to sixth order. Anisotropy is how strongly a magnet's magnetization prefers certain crystal directions.

Ada: Does it get applied to real compounds?

Ray: No abstract is available, so I can't say. We only have the title and the authors.

Ray: Next, an experimental check. A Physical Review Materials paper studied iron cobalt phosphorus silicon compounds, in the Fe two P family, using X ray absorption, X ray linear dichroism, and neutron powder diffraction. The aim is to learn which sites the cobalt and silicon occupy, and what magnetic structures result.

Ada: And what did they find?

Ray: The excerpt is truncated, so the magnetic findings aren't in my text. The setup is what I can give you.

Ray: Third, a machine learning one. Researchers used expert preferences, learned from pairwise comparisons, to guide a crystal diffusion model looking for flat electronic bands. Experts mostly agreed with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements were systematic, and not explained by an estimated five percent rate of mistaken labels.

Ada: So what did the preferences find that the score missed?

Ray: They favored potassium cobalt two arsenic two and cobalt gallium, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. This is about flat bands, not magnetism, so any magnetic use would be our inference.

Metal printing

Ray: Metal printing. ABS and Radian Forge, based in Portsmouth, Virginia, signed a joint development project to see whether digital manufacturing data can qualify parts made by wire arc additive manufacturing, which builds parts by depositing weld metal. It's framed as a condition for wider use of additive manufacturing at sea.

Ada: What sensors? What's the ground truth?

Ray: The item doesn't say. Details are thin.

Ray: Next, melt pool prediction in laser powder bed fusion. Researchers tested whether two dimensionless features, normalized enthalpy and Peclet number, beat raw process parameters across seven models, including three pretrained tabular foundation models. Materials were three sixteen L stainless steel, Inconel six twenty five, and Inconel seven eighteen.

Ada: And the headline number?

Ray: Dimensionless features were comparable or better in most settings, with the biggest gain in cross material depth prediction, an R squared of zero point nine six. But it predicts from process parameters, not sensor signals.

Ray: Last, federated learning for thermal simulation. Sites train models on their own part geometries and share only the model pieces. On a two dimensional steady state benchmark across three sites, errors were one point eight three to two point zero four percent, versus up to twenty point four six percent for local only training.

Ada: Simplified benchmark, simulation surrogate, not monitoring. Noted.

Weird physics corner

Ray: Time for the weird stuff. Can a machine provably discover new quantum phases of matter? One paper says yes, under physically motivated assumptions.

Ada: Provably? That's a bold word.

Ray: It is. The quantum algorithm takes a family of local Hamiltonians and some unverified reference ground states. No order parameter, no training data. It moves each state through parameter space and taps it with a frequency filtered probe. If the energy gap closes, the probe creates excitations, and that flags a phase boundary with a verifiable certificate.

Ada: So a quantum computer needed. Not something I'm running on my laptop.

Ray: Right, it's a quantum algorithm under stated assumptions, not a ready tool.

Ray: And one more. In an eternal black hole, entanglement between the two sides is tied to a geometric bridge. A neural network learned the black hole metric from how entanglement entropy changes over time. With one unknown function, it recovers the metric, even part of the interior. With two unknowns, it can't, because physically different geometries give the same signal.

Ada: I love a machine that admits it's confused. Relatable.

Policy and money

Ray: Briskly now. USA Rare Earth began commercial scale heavy rare earth shipments, per Yahoo Finance. Heavy rare earths matter for high temperature permanent magnets. Only the headline is available, so volumes and elements are unconfirmed.

Ada: And the context?

Ray: One report says a China rare earth truce is nearing expiry. Another says defense giants have forty five days to prove their magnets are China free. A third says military drones face limits on Chinese magnets starting in twenty twenty seven. All headline only, so dates and terms are unverified.

Ray: In additive manufacturing, Velo3D was selected for a ten million dollar award from the DEVCOM Armaments Center, and the Department of War and Commerce launched a survey on additive manufacturing barriers. Scope and deadlines aren't in what we have.

Fun fact

Ray: Fun fact time. Theory predicts that when a disordered quantum gas condenses into a Bose Einstein condensate, a tangle of tiny vortices forms and gradually unravels.

Ada: And?

Ray: Phys.org reports that this process was caught happening in an ultracold gas.

Euler-characteristic observable tested for Ising criticality with reweighting and FSS

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 7/10

The abstract reports a spin-odd topological observable, built from domain cell complexes, that behaves like an order parameter near the transition. Using multihistogram reweighting and finite-size scaling, the authors recover the known critical temperature on square and triangular lattices. A reported caveat is that exponent estimates depend more on the fitting range than magnetization does, which points to stronger subleading corrections.

ABS and Radian Forge test sensor data as qualification evidence for WAAM parts

3D Printing Industry · 7/10

The item says the joint project will evaluate whether digital manufacturing data can qualify metal parts made by wire-arc additive manufacturing (WAAM), which builds parts by depositing weld metal. The effort is framed as a condition for wider use in maritime applications. Details are thin, so the sensors and ground truth they plan to use are unconfirmed.

Algorithm certifies quantum phase boundaries by detecting gap closing, with no labels

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 7/10

The abstract describes an algorithm that maps the phase diagram of a family of quantum Hamiltonians without order parameters or training data. It transports reference ground states and uses a frequency-filtered probe to witness gap closing, producing a verifiable certificate for each reported transition. It is framed as a quantum algorithm under stated assumptions, so it is not a ready-to-use tool.

USA Rare Earth begins commercial-scale heavy rare-earth shipments

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 8/10

Yahoo Finance reports commercial-scale shipments of heavy rare earths, elements that are important for high-temperature permanent magnets. Only the headline is available, so volumes and specific elements are unconfirmed. A separate NAI500 report says a China rare-earth truce is nearing expiry.

Anisotropy energy functions derived for all point groups to sixth order

J. Magnetism & Magnetic Materials · 7/10

The title points to symmetry-constrained functions describing magnetocrystalline anisotropy, which is how strongly a magnet's magnetization prefers certain crystal directions. No abstract is available, so the scope and any application to real compounds are unconfirmed.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Site-selective Co/Si substitution in Fe2P-type compounds probed by XLD and neutrons

Physical Review Materials · 7/10

The item reports a combined X-ray absorption (XAS) and X-ray linear dichroism (XLD) study, plus neutron diffraction, of how cobalt and silicon occupy sites in Fe-Co-P-Si compounds and what magnetic structures result. Linking atomic site occupancy to magnetic order is the kind of experimental check that helps validate computational predictions. The excerpt is truncated, so the magnetic findings are unconfirmed.

Expert preferences guide crystal diffusion where numerical rewards miss candidates

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports that experts' disagreements with a bandwidth score are systematic, and that preferences learned from pairwise comparisons can steer a crystal diffusion model. The target in this work is flat electronic bands rather than magnetism. Applying the idea to magnetic targets would be an inference, not a claim of the paper.

LLM agent speeds Quantum ESPRESSO relaxation and predicts bands

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 5/10

The abstract reports a 2.75-fold speedup in structural relaxation for Quantum ESPRESSO, a widely used density-functional theory code, and a band model with 0.157 eV median error on held-out compositions, including lanthanides and magnetic compounds. Band energies are a different quantity from magnetic anisotropy, so the relevance to magnetic properties is limited. The summary doesn't detail how the magnetic and f-electron cases were treated.

Attractive-polaron phase diagram gives sharper bound on Nagaoka ferromagnetism instability

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 5/10

The abstract reports that Yang's eta dimer, an exact eigenstate that maps onto the Nagaoka ferromagnet, yields a rigorous criterion for when that ferromagnetic state becomes unstable. The setting is cold-atom lattice theory rather than solid materials. It is a mechanism-level result, not a materials one.

Additive Manufacturing

Dimensionless features improve cross-material melt pool prediction across tabular models

arXiv · AM monitoring & physics · 6/10

The abstract reports that normalized enthalpy and Peclet number give comparable or better predictions than raw process parameters, with the largest gain in cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96). The study covers 316L, IN625 and IN718. It predicts from process parameters rather than sensor signals, so it is best read as a feature-engineering idea.

Velo3D selected for $10M DEVCOM Armaments Center award

TCT Magazine · 6/10

TCT reports an Other Transaction Authority award from the DEVCOM Armaments Center, a mechanism for moving commercial technology into defense use. It is a defense-sector additive manufacturing contract signal. Details on scope are limited.

DoW and Commerce launch survey on additive manufacturing barriers

News · AM policy & funding · 6/10

ExecutiveGov reports a federal survey, from the Department of War (DoW) and Commerce, on barriers to additive manufacturing. Surveys like this can shape future funding priorities. Only the headline is available, so the deadline and who can respond are unconfirmed.

Federated physics-informed operators predict thermal fields on unseen geometries

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 5/10

The abstract reports errors of 1.83% to 2.04%, versus up to 20.46% for local-only training, on a 2D steady-state benchmark spread across three sites. The work is a simulation surrogate, not a monitoring method. The benchmark is a simplified 2D case.

Theoretical Physics

Critical droplet size in long-range Ising chains changes at sigma = 1

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

In a nearest-neighbor Ising chain, a droplet's domain-wall cost doesn't depend on its size. With 1/r^(1+sigma) interactions it does, and the abstract reports a critical radius scaling as h^(-1/sigma) at small bias field, with sigma = 1 separating two regimes. It is theory about how magnetic systems decay from metastable states, not tied to any particular material.

Ring exchange in triangular molecular magnets can drive photon condensation

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 6/10

The abstract derives, from the half-filled Hubbard model, an effective Hamiltonian in which virtual ring exchange couples cavity light to scalar spin chirality. In plain terms, a magnetic property that is not simple spin alignment can order together with light in a cavity. It is a theoretical exchange-mechanism idea, not a materials result.

Neural ODE reconstructs black-hole geometry from entanglement entropy over time

arXiv · high-energy theory · 6/10

The idea is that in a black hole, entanglement between the two sides is tied to a geometric bridge (ER=EPR), so how entanglement evolves over time carries information about the interior. The abstract reports that a neural network recovers the metric when one function is unknown, but not when two are unknown, because different geometries produce the same signal. That limit is the notable part.

New theorem limits how far quantum observers can disagree

Phys.org · Quantum physics · 5/10

According to a Phys.org summary, two observers who share the same description and probability rules can still disagree about an outcome's chance while being certain of each other's assessments. A new theorem sets limits on how far such disagreement can go. Only the summary is available, so the exact bound is unconfirmed.
